title: One of the Twelve

story: One of the Twelve, named in every list as James the son of Alphaeus; Scripture records nothing he said or did.

entries.title: Never named again
entries.text: The last verse that names him is Acts 1:13. After that Acts speaks of “the eleven” and “the twelve” as a body (Acts 2:14; 6:2) but never names him again.

entries.title: Another James leads at Jerusalem
entries.text: A James later leads the church in Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18), and Paul speaks of “James the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19). Whether that James is this apostle is disputed; see below.

verses.text: Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
And Simon he surnamed Peter;
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.

items.q: Is James son of Alphaeus the same man as “James the Lord's brother”?
items.full: Is James son of Alphaeus the same man as “James the Lord's brother”? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Two different men
views.holders: Helvidius (about AD 380), who took the Lord's brothers as later sons of Joseph and Mary; the older view, first found in the apocryphal Gospel of James (its stories go back to the 2nd century), that they were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage; A. C. McGiffert (1890); Philip Schaff (1890)

argument.text: John says the Lord's brothers did not believe in him after the Twelve had been chosen, and Acts names the apostles and then, separately, “his brethren”.

Paul counts “James the Lord's brother” among the apostles he saw, and there were only two apostles named James; so Jerome took the Lord's brothers to be cousins, sons of the Mary who was the wife of Clopas.

items.q: Is Alphaeus the same man as Clopas (KJV “Cleophas”), husband of a Mary at the cross?
items.full: Is Alphaeus the same man as Clopas (KJV “Cleophas”), husband of a Mary at the cross? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: The same man
views.holders: John Chrysostom, as reported by A. W. Fortune (ISBE, 1915); Smith (1884); Easton (1897)

argument.text: The two names may be forms of one Aramaic name, and the Mary of Clopas may be the Mary who was mother of James.

views.label: Not proven, or different men
views.holders: A. W. Fortune (ISBE, 1915), who still thinks it “quite probable”; Renan, whose separation of the names McGiffert (1890) finds there is “much to be said” for

argument.text: The link rests on several steps that cannot be proved: that the two Marys are one, that her son James is the apostle, and that the names are one name.

items.q: Does Paul count James among the apostles in Galatians 1:19?
items.full: Does Paul count James among the apostles in Galatians 1:19? (Most widely held view first.)
items.from: Asked on James, the Lord's brother’s page

views.label: Yes: an apostle, but not one of the Twelve
views.holders: J. B. Lightfoot (1890); Eusebius (about 325), who says many besides the Twelve “were called apostles”

argument.text: Lightfoot reads “other of the apostles saw I none, save James” as naming James an apostle; the same James is not in the lists of the Twelve, and Acts 1:13-14 names the brothers apart from the apostles.

views.label: Yes, because he was one of the Twelve: James son of Alphaeus
views.holders: Jerome, Against Helvidius 15 (about AD 383); Clement of Alexandria (about 200), as McGiffert reads him

argument.text: If Paul calls him an apostle, and only two of the Twelve were named James, the Lord's brother must be the son of Alphaeus.

items.q: Who were “the brethren of the Lord”?
items.full: Who were “the brethren of the Lord”? (In the order the views arose.)
items.from: Asked on James, the Lord's brother’s page

views.label: Sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage
views.holders: First found in the apocryphal Protevangelium of James (its stories go back to the 2nd century), where Joseph says “I have children”; Origen (about AD 245 or later), who reports that “some say” it, “basing it on a tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is entitled, or ‘The Book of James’”; Eusebius (about 325), for whom James “was known as a son of Joseph”; some in Jerome's day (“as some think”); J. B. Lightfoot (1865, 10th ed. 1890), “the strongest advocate” of it in McGiffert's words; still the established view of the Greek Church, McGiffert (1890) notes

argument.text: Lightfoot's chief argument: on the cross Jesus gave his mother to “the disciple … whom he loved”, and “from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home” (John 19:26-27), which he finds hard to believe if she had sons of her own. McGiffert grants that this view “has the oldest tradition in its favor”, though none of the traditions, he adds, is old enough “to be of great weight”.

views.label: Younger sons of Joseph and Mary
views.holders: Tertullian (early 3rd century), whose argument, Lightfoot judges, “seems to imply” it; Helvidius (about 380), against whom Jerome wrote; A. C. McGiffert (1890), who names Andrews, Schaff and Weiss with him and notes that the view is “widely accepted in the Protestant Church”; H. E. Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: The plain sense of “brother” and “sisters” beside “his mother” (Mark 6:3); Mary's “firstborn son” (Luke 2:7); and the brothers' unbelief (John 7:5), which, McGiffert argues, keeps them out of the Twelve.

views.label: Cousins: the sons of Mary the wife of Clopas
views.holders: Jerome, Against Helvidius (about AD 383); since then the established view of the Latin Church, McGiffert (1890) notes; W. H. Mill (1843), as reported by Lightfoot and McGiffert

argument.text: Jerome argues that Paul counts “James the Lord's brother” among the apostles, that only two apostles were called James, and so the Lord's “brethren” were kinsmen, sons of the Mary who stood at the cross (John 19:25).

items.q: Which James wrote the letter of James?
items.full: Which James wrote the letter of James?
items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: James the Lord's brother, a son of Joseph and Mary (the "Helvidian" view, after Helvidius, 4th century)
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1892), who examines all three theories of the Lord's brothers

argument.text: The plain reading of Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 names James as a brother of Jesus. Because the brothers did not believe in him during his ministry, they cannot have been among the Twelve; the risen Jesus appeared to James, and Paul calls him "the Lord's brother" and a "pillar" of the Jerusalem church.

views.label: The Lord's brother as a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the "Epiphanian" view, after Epiphanius, a 4th-century bishop)
views.holders: Examined by Mayor; Bigg reports that Clement of Alexandria held it of Jude, following the tradition in the Protevangelium of James; Eusebius says only that James was called the Lord's brother as a son of Joseph

argument.text: An early tradition that keeps the brothers as real family of Joseph's household while preserving Mary's virginity.

views.label: A cousin, the same man as James the son of Alphaeus, one of the Twelve (the "Hieronymian" view, after Jerome)
views.holders: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men ch. 2; Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897)

argument.text: "Brother" is read in the wider sense of kinsman: Jerome made James the son of a sister of the Lord's mother, which lets the writer be one of the apostles.

views.label: Undecided between the son of Alphaeus and a Jerusalem leader

argument.text: Calvin thought the "pillar" of Galatians 2:9 was more likely the apostle, the son of Alphaeus, because he doubted a non-apostle would rank above apostles — but he declined to say which James wrote the letter.

views.label: A later writer using the name, or a Jewish work lightly made Christian
views.holders: Spitta (a Jewish treatise with "Jesus Christ" added at 1:1 and 2:1), as reported by the ISBE; Davidson, Hilgenfeld, Baur, Zeller, Hausrath, von Soden, Jülicher, Harnack and Bacon, who dated it between about 70 and 150

argument.text: The letter has little explicit Christian teaching and is written in good Greek.

items.q: Scripture tells nothing of his home, his trade, his calling or anything he said: he is a name in the lists.
No verse calls the son of Alphaeus “James the less”; that is an identification.
Scripture does not say where he went after Pentecost or how he died.
